strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: reducing learning-rate tuning for sign-based optimization in single-node and distributed settings.
Proposes both a search-based method and an inexpensive-to-compute local adaptation rule, with substantial theoretical development.
Includes experiments on logistic regression, 130M-parameter language-model pretraining, and Swin fine-tuning, with AdamW and Prodigy comparisons. ALIAS Adam achieves competitive reported accuracy.
weaknesses: The central stochastic complexity claim is not established. Theorem 3 claims an iteration bound for reaching epsilon accuracy, but its proof in Appendix E.2 retains a nonvanishing noise term. A bound of the form A/sqrt(T) + B cannot imply arbitrary epsilon accuracy by adding B squared to the iteration complexity. The text acknowledges convergence only to a neighborhood, contradicting the theorem statement; analogous errors appear in the stochastic SOS and distributed results.

Algorithm 4 is undefined at initialization: its denominator is an empty sum at t=0, giving an infinite step size. The proof also incorrectly lower-bounds this empty sum by L_infinity^0. No finite initialization procedure is specified. Moreover, smoothness and convexity do not ensure positive local curvature or finite inverse-curvature moments required by the bounds.

The deterministic Option II guarantee drops an essential dependence. Appendix E.1 derives a bound involving f(x0) minus the supplied lower bound, then replaces this quantity with Delta* without controlling the approximation error. An arbitrary lower bound on the optimum does not justify that replacement.

The parameter-free and near-optimal claims require substantial qualification. SOS requires initialization conditions involving unknown problem quantities, while ALIAS Option I retains an unfavorable Delta*/d0 factor and both options incur local-curvature dependence. The best empirical variant additionally uses a prescribed learning-rate multiplier and a cosine schedule, with no convergence analysis connecting Algorithm 5 to the proved algorithms.

The empirical superiority evidence is limited. The best language-model loss improves from 2.923 to 2.918 over tuned Sign-SGD, and Swin accuracy from 78.885% to 79.161%, without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. All language-model experiments also optimize the LM head with AdamW. Initialization sensitivity, complete tuning ranges, and controlled ablations of the proposed adaptation are missing.

The efficiency and distributed motivation is insufficiently demonstrated. Table 3 reports ALIAS Adam using more memory and roughly 4.3 times the per-iteration time of AdamW; basic ALIAS also increases memory and time over Sign-SGD. There are no communication-volume or distributed scaling comparisons validating the proposed compressed algorithms. The reported DDP runs do not establish those benefits.

strengths: Addresses a relevant optimization problem: reducing learning-rate tuning for sign-based methods used in memory-constrained and distributed training.
Proposes two complementary approaches, trajectory-based stepsize search and per-iteration adaptation, with substantial analysis of deterministic, stochastic, and distributed settings.

Includes experiments beyond toy problems: 130M-parameter language-model pretraining and Swin fine-tuning. ALIAS Adam with cosine scheduling achieves the best reported results, and comparisons include tuned Sign-SGD, AdamW, and Prodigy.
weaknesses: The stochastic complexity guarantee is not supported by its proof. Theorem 3 claims an iteration bound for reaching arbitrary epsilon accuracy, but Appendix E.2, equation (61), retains a nonvanishing noise term. Increasing iterations cannot remove this floor; the complexity must restrict epsilon relative to the floor or change the sampling scheme. Section 3.2.1 acknowledges neighborhood convergence without correcting the theorem. The inverse-curvature moments appearing in the bound are also not guaranteed finite by the stated assumptions.

ALIAS Sign-SGD is undefined at initialization as written. Algorithm 4 computes lambda at t=0 using the reciprocal square root of an empty sum, producing an infinite stepsize. The proof on page 40 likewise bounds this denominator below by the first local curvature even for t=0. A finite initialization and its contribution to the bound are needed. Smooth convex functions can also have zero local curvature away from an optimum, so division by local curvature requires explicit treatment.

The Option II guarantee incorrectly removes dependence on the supplied objective lower bound. On page 42, the proof obtains a rate depending on f(x0) minus the supplied lower bound, then replaces this quantity with Delta*. An arbitrary lower bound can be arbitrarily loose; the stated assumptions do not justify that replacement. Theorem 2 therefore needs an additional approximation-quality assumption or a weaker bound.

The parameter-free and near-optimality claims need substantial qualification. SOS requires an initial search interval whose sufficient conditions depend on unknown problem quantities, without a complete adaptive interval-expansion procedure in Algorithm 3. ALIAS Option I retains a Delta*/d0 penalty, and both options incur a potentially unbounded squared global-to-initial-local-curvature ratio. The stronger rate in Remark 1 explicitly requires the unknown global smoothness constant.

The strongest empirical results concern an Adam-style heuristic that is not covered by the convergence analysis. Algorithm 5 introduces moment estimates, a different adaptation rule, and an external stepsize; Appendix A.2 selects this stepsize as 10^-3. Its connection to the analyzed ALIAS algorithm needs justification and ablation. Cosine scheduling and tuned weight decay remain important, and the language-model head uses AdamW for every method, limiting claims of tuning-free training.

The experiments establish competitiveness more convincingly than superiority. In Table 2, the best validation loss improves from 2.923 for tuned Sign-SGD to 2.918; in Table 5, accuracy improves from 78.885% to 79.161%. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported. Basic ALIAS also underperforms tuned cosine Sign-SGD in Table 1. Initialization sensitivity, the contribution of individual adaptation components, and total tuning cost are not adequately evaluated.

The resource-efficiency and distributed-training motivation is insufficiently validated. Table 3 reports ALIAS Adam using more memory than AdamW and approximately 4.3 times its per-iteration time. Stochastic ALIAS requires two gradient evaluations per iteration, but the relationship between training steps, plotted gradient calls, and compute budgets is unclear. Ordinary DistributedDataParallel runs do not establish the benefits of the proposed compressed majority-vote algorithms; communication-volume and scaling experiments are missing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code-availability statement contains no link, learning-rate search ranges and selected settings are not fully specified, and important initialization and numerical-stabilization details are absent. These omissions are particularly consequential because the pseudocode cannot be implemented literally without resolving the issues above.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: reducing learning-rate tuning for sign-based optimization in single-node and distributed settings.
The objective-gap estimator and local smoothness adaptation provide concrete algorithmic ideas, supported by substantial theoretical development.
Experiments cover logistic regression, 130M-parameter language-model pretraining, and Swin fine-tuning, with relevant comparisons against tuned Sign-SGD, AdamW, and Prodigy.
The scheduled ALIAS Adam variant achieves promising results: language-model validation loss of 2.918 versus 2.929 for AdamW, and Tiny ImageNet accuracy of 79.161% versus 78.885% for tuned Sign-SGD.
weaknesses: The stochastic guarantee is not supported as stated. Theorem 3 claims an iteration bound for reaching arbitrary epsilon accuracy, but its proof in Appendix E.2 retains a nonvanishing noise term. Such a bound requires an explicit accuracy restriction relative to the noise floor; the discussion acknowledges this limitation without correcting the theorem.

The Option II guarantees incorrectly replace the computable gap f(x0) minus the supplied lower bound with the true gap Delta*. Appendices E.1 and E.2 derive bounds involving the former, which can be arbitrarily larger. Merely assuming a valid lower bound does not justify the stated dependence on Delta*.

Algorithm 4 is undefined at initialization: its stepsize denominator is an empty sum at t=0. Subsequent guarantees also require positive local curvature and finite inverse-curvature moments, neither ensured by the assumptions. An explicit initialization and treatment of zero curvature are necessary.

The parameter-free and near-optimal claims need qualification. SOS requires initialization conditions involving unknown problem quantities. ALIAS Option I assumes d0 < Delta* and incurs an additional Delta*/d0 factor, while both options incur potentially large curvature-ratio penalties. The small empirical sensitivity study does not establish that these penalties are generally negligible.

The strongest empirical results concern Algorithm 5, an Adam-like variant without a corresponding convergence guarantee. It retains two moment vectors and an externally specified learning-rate multiplier of 0.001; its best results additionally use cosine scheduling. The relationship between this variant, the analyzed ALIAS algorithm, and existing adaptive Adam methods needs clearer justification and ablation.

Empirical superiority is not established robustly: no seed variability or confidence intervals are reported despite small improvements over the strongest baselines. All language-model runs also optimize the LM head with AdamW, limiting claims of fully tuning-free training. The code-availability statement contains no link, and initialization and tuning details are incomplete.

The efficiency and distributed-learning motivation lacks convincing validation. Table 3 reports that ALIAS Adam uses more memory and optimizer time than AdamW, and stochastic ALIAS requires two gradient evaluations per iteration. There is no dedicated communication-compression or multi-node scaling evaluation; ordinary DistributedDataParallel runs do not demonstrate the proposed distributed method's benefit.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reducing learning-rate tuning costs while retaining the practical advantages of sign-based optimization. Accumulating local smoothness estimates and estimating the objective gap provides a concrete algorithmic contribution.

The empirical evaluation covers 130M and 350M language models, Swin fine-tuning, and two AlgoPerf tasks, with comparisons against AdamW, Prodigy, DoG, D-Adaptation, and MoMo. The scheduled ALIAS Adam variant achieves competitive reported results.
The appendix provides useful ablations on batch size, initialization, smoothness regularization, and the memory-saving approximation, together with optimizer memory and timing measurements.
weaknesses: The stochastic iteration-complexity claim is not supported by its proof. Equation (61) contains a noise term that does not decay with T, yet Theorem 3.9 converts it into an additive iteration count and claims epsilon accuracy without requiring epsilon to exceed the noise floor. The discussion acknowledges neighborhood convergence, but this does not correct the theorem. Analogous problems occur in the distributed analysis.

The deterministic Option II guarantee incorrectly removes dependence on the supplied lower bound. On page 43, the proof establishes a rate involving f(x0) minus the lower bound, then replaces this quantity with Delta* merely because the lower bound approximates the optimum. An arbitrary valid lower bound can be arbitrarily loose; the stated assumptions do not justify this replacement.

The algorithms and guarantees need explicit initialization and nondegeneracy conditions. Algorithms 2 and 7 access x(-1) and its gradient without defining them, while the equivalent accumulated-smoothness expression has an empty denominator initially. Subsequent guarantees involve inverse local curvature and inverse minimum sampled curvature, whose finiteness is not ensured by smoothness and convexity.

The theory does not cover the most important practical variants. The stochastic analysis treats Option II, whereas experiments use Option I; the memory-saving approximation is explicitly excluded from its theorem; and the strongest empirical method, ALIAS Adam, lacks a convergence analysis. Moreover, the memory-section claim L_infinity <= d L_1 is false in general under the stated definitions: f(x) = (sum_i x_i)^2/2 has L_infinity = d^2 and L_1 = 1.

The scope of the parameter-free claim is insufficiently established. ALIAS Adam uses an externally selected multiplier gamma = 10^-3, its strongest results require cosine scheduling, weight decay is selected by validation, and all language-model experiments optimize the LM head with AdamW. These choices can be reasonable, but require sensitivity experiments and clearer qualification of exactly which tuning is eliminated.

The approximately 1.5x end-to-end speedup claimed in the abstract is not substantiated by a reproducible tuning-cost comparison. Search endpoints, trial counts, early-stopping policies, and total GPU-hours are missing. Table 4 reports higher per-iteration optimizer time for ALIAS Adam than AdamW, and the stochastic ALIAS method requires two gradient queries per iteration, making explicit accounting of updates, oracle calls, and wall-clock time essential.

Reported superiority is not statistically established: no repeated-seed variability or confidence intervals accompany the small language-model gains, such as 2.918 versus 2.929 validation loss. Some AlgoPerf baselines are imported from another paper rather than rerun, and there are no distributed communication or scaling experiments. The empirical evidence supports promise, but does not resolve the theoretical and efficiency concerns sufficiently for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: reducing learning-rate tuning for sign-based optimization while considering optimizer memory costs. Accumulating local smoothness estimates provides a concrete algorithmic contribution.
The empirical evaluation includes LLaMA models at two sizes, Swin fine-tuning, and two additional AlgoPerf tasks. Comparisons include tuned AdamW, Sign-SGD, Prodigy, DoG, D-Adaptation, and MoMo.

The reported results are promising: scheduled ALIAS Adam achieves validation losses of 2.918 versus AdamW's 2.929 at 130M parameters and 2.707 versus 2.719 at 350M. The appendix also investigates memory consumption, gradient noise, and approximation quality.
weaknesses: The stochastic convergence theorem is not supported as stated. The proof of Theorem F.6 produces a nonvanishing noise term, but Theorem 3.9 claims an iteration bound for reaching arbitrary epsilon accuracy without requiring epsilon to exceed this noise floor. The discussion acknowledges convergence only to a neighborhood, contradicting the formal statement. Moreover, the inverse local-smoothness moments appearing in the bounds are not guaranteed finite by the stated assumptions.

The deterministic guarantees also need correction. Algorithms 2 and 7 start at t=0 but require an unspecified x^{-1}; the corresponding proof uses a reciprocal empty sum at t=0. No initialization or zero-curvature safeguard resolves this. For Option II, the proof obtains dependence on f(x0) minus the supplied lower bound, then replaces it with Delta* without assuming the lower bound is sufficiently tight. An arbitrary lower bound does not justify the advertised dependence.

The strongest empirical method is insufficiently connected to the central theory. Algorithm 3 introduces Adam moments and an external learning-rate multiplier, omits the accumulated local-smoothness estimator central to Algorithm 2, and has no convergence analysis. The practical stochastic Option I is also explicitly outside the stochastic analysis. Consequently, the guarantees do not establish the behavior of the variants responsible for the strongest experimental results.

The memory-efficient theory does not cover the implemented approximation. The analyzed norm difference still requires the previous full gradient, whereas the implementation uses coordinate extrema. This surrogate can remain positive even when two gradient vectors are identical, so a general approximation-quality argument is needed. There is also an incorrect norm comparison: Section 3.3 states L_infinity <= d L_1, whereas f(x) = (sum_i x_i)^2/2 has L_1 = 1 and L_infinity = d^2 under the paper's definitions.

The approximately 1.5x end-to-end speedup claimed in the abstract lacks a documented tuning-budget and wall-clock comparison. Table 4 instead reports larger per-iteration costs for ALIAS and ALIAS Adam than for Sign-SGD and AdamW. Avoiding tuning could offset this overhead, but establishing that requires search ranges, trial counts, stopping rules, and total compute measurements.

The parameter-free and superiority claims exceed the experimental evidence. ALIAS Adam uses a fixed multiplier of 10^-3, its best results use a manually specified cosine schedule, weight decay is validation-selected, and the language-model head is trained with AdamW. These choices do not invalidate learning-rate adaptation, but their sensitivity and tuning costs need accounting. Without cosine scheduling, ALIAS Adam's 130M loss is 2.976 rather than 2.918.

Reported improvements lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates, making small differences difficult to interpret. The learning-rate grid spacing is given without its range or full selected configurations, and the AlgoPerf baseline results are imported from another study without sufficient evidence of matched evaluation budgets. These limitations weaken both reproducibility and the claimed advantage over existing parameter-free optimizers.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful practical problem: reducing learning-rate tuning costs while retaining the simplicity and potential memory savings of sign-based optimization. Accumulating local smoothness estimates provides a plausible adaptive mechanism.

The empirical evaluation is broader than the main text alone suggests, covering 130M and 350M language models, Swin fine-tuning, and two AlgoPerf tasks. Comparisons include tuned sign methods, AdamW, Prodigy, DoG, D-Adaptation, and MoMo.

The Adam-style variant produces competitive results: validation losses of 2.918 versus AdamW's 2.929 at 130M, and 2.707 versus 2.719 at 350M. The memory-efficient variant also demonstrates a useful empirical tradeoff between storage and performance.
The appendices provide extensive derivations and useful ablations on gradient noise, initialization, smoothness offsets, and the memory-saving approximation.
weaknesses: The stated guarantees contain substantive gaps. In Theorem 3.5, Option II permits any lower bound on the optimal objective, but its proof on page 43 derives dependence on f(x0) minus that lower bound, then replaces this quantity by the potentially much smaller true optimality gap without justification. Theorem 3.9 also states an iteration complexity for reaching epsilon accuracy despite its accompanying discussion acknowledging a nonvanishing noise floor; the required accuracy restriction is missing. These are consequential issues in the central theoretical claims.

The algorithms and guarantees need explicit initialization and nondegeneracy conditions. Algorithms 2 and 7 initialize the smoothness accumulator at zero but immediately reference an unspecified previous iterate. Their bounds involve inverse initial or minimum local curvature, which need not be positive or have finite inverse moments under the stated assumptions. Smooth convex objectives can have locally affine regions, so these cases cannot simply be excluded implicitly.

There is a substantial gap between the analyzed and evaluated methods. The stochastic analysis covers Option II, whereas Algorithm 7 identifies Option I as the practical version. The memory-efficient theorem analyzes the exact gradient-difference norm rather than the implemented extrema approximation. The strongest empirical results use Algorithm 3, whose Adam-style update has no accompanying convergence guarantee or clear derivation from the analyzed local-smoothness mechanism.

The claim of eliminating stepsize selection needs qualification. Algorithm 3 retains an external stepsize, set to 0.001 in the experiments, and its best results use cosine scheduling. Language-model experiments additionally optimize the LM head with AdamW, while weight decay is selected through validation. These choices do not invalidate learning-rate adaptation, but sensitivity to the remaining stepsize and the tuning requirements of the hybrid optimizer are not adequately established.

The approximately 1.5× end-to-end speedup asserted in the abstract is not supported by a reproducible tuning-inclusive timing comparison. Table 4 instead reports higher per-iteration time for ALIAS Adam than AdamW (0.03 versus 0.007 seconds). Search ranges, trial counts, stopping policies, and aggregate tuning costs are missing, making the claimed savings impossible to assess reliably.

The small empirical advantages are reported without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. For example, the 130M loss improvement over MoMo is only 0.007, and the Swin accuracy improvement over tuned sign-SGD is 0.276 percentage points. AlgoPerf baselines are imported from another study, and there is no distributed communication or scaling experiment despite the distributed motivation. Overall, the promising results do not yet compensate for the unresolved theoretical and evaluation issues at a top-tier acceptance threshold.
